title: Paint protection choices: wax, sealant and coating
audience: Car detailers who recommend and apply protection to paint, and who explain its durability to owners.
learningOutcomes: Compare natural wax, synthetic sealant and coating on durability, application method and maintenance.
Prepare the paint before protection, including removing residues that would stop the protection bonding.
Apply protection thinly, observe the label's cure and levelling times, and state only the durability the maker supports.

instruction.heading: Protection is a layer, not a repair
instruction.body: Protection sits on top of the paint and does not repair it. The show-car sample says clear coat still needs washing, clay, polishing and protection on a regular schedule to keep its appearance, and that a clear layer is not an invisible force field. Protection products do three jobs: they add gloss and depth, they make dirt release more easily, and they shield the surface from sun and weather. Each type does those jobs differently and for a different time. Choose the product from the owner's use of the car (garage or outdoor parking, daily driving or shows), the paint's condition, the time available for application, and the owner's budget. A protective layer over damaged paint seals the damage in, so the condition record from “Vehicle condition and evidence” and the polishing decision in “Polishing and paint correction: the difference” come first.

instruction.heading: Natural wax
instruction.body: Carnauba wax is the classic natural product. The Auto-Detailing guide describes it as giving a deep, wet look and good water beading, but as lasting three to eight weeks, depending on use and conditions. The Spanish-language manual says natural waxes are applied by hand, because machine heat can soften the wax before it is spread thinly. Apply a very thin layer, allow it to dry for the label's time, and remove the residue with a clean microfibre towel. The guide's example is 10 to 20 minutes before buffing, but the label governs. Work in shade. Two or three thin coats can add depth, but each coat needs its own cure time, and a wax does not level swirls. A wax suits the owner who wants a short-term, deep finish, such as before a show.

instruction.heading: Synthetic sealant
instruction.body: Synthetic sealants are polymer products. The Auto-Detailing guide describes them as lasting about three to six months, longer than carnauba, and as applied by hand or with a dual-action or random orbital polisher fitted with a soft foam pad. Spread the product as thinly and as far as possible, and remove the excess after the label's time. The guide suggests at least one hour before a second coat, and a longer wait is safer. The Spanish-language manual warns that a sealant left too long before removal becomes much harder to take off, so timing matters. A sealant can be topped with a wax for extra gloss. The guide suggests reapplying a sealant about once a season, or sooner when water stops beading and begins to pool.

instruction.heading: Coatings
instruction.body: Coatings are semi-permanent layers, usually applied panel by panel because they dry quickly. The Auto-Detailing guide describes a timer-led process: apply a few drops to an applicator, work the coating in thinly, and level it with a clean towel within the window the label allows. A coating that dries too far before it is levelled leaves haze that may need polishing out. The Car-Detailing-Guide says most manufacturers want 24 hours before water exposure and no detergent washing for four to seven days, with full cure in one to four weeks. The Spanish manual gives 12 to 24 hours depending on humidity. The label governs. A second layer usually has to go on within a stated window, often 30 to 60 minutes, or it will not bond. The guide gives a life of one to three years or more, but that is the manufacturer's claim and must be presented as one. Do not clay a coated surface; the guide says clay can diminish the coating, and suggests iron and tar removers instead. Heat lamps to speed the cure are not adopted in this lesson.

instruction.heading: Choosing and what you may promise
instruction.body: Match the type to the owner's use. A car parked outdoors under trees gains more from a longer-lasting layer, while a short show finish suits a wax. Explain that durability depends on washing, parking, weather and the state of the paint at application. The durability of any product is the maker's figure, and the business must be able to support what it tells the owner. The ACCC guidance says claims must be accurate and backed by evidence the business can produce, and that intent does not matter when a claim misleads. Do not promise lifetime protection, a never-polish result, or a fixed number of months unless the maker's documentation supports it and the owner has the same information.

procedure: Record the paint condition and agree the protection with the owner, including the car's use and the time available.
Wash, decontaminate and polish as agreed, and degrease only where the protection is meant to bond after the degreaser.
Confirm the surface is dry, clean and free of residue, and check it by touch.
Apply the chosen product thinly, panel by panel, using the method for its type.
Remove or level the residue within the label's time, using a clean towel.
Allow the label's cure time before washing or applying a second coat.
Record the product, the cure time and any instruction given to the owner.

workedExamples.situation: A car parked outdoors under trees has been polished. The owner wants protection that lasts through summer and asks for lifetime protection.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which protection do you recommend, and what do you say about durability?
workedExamples.reasoning: Outdoor parking and tree sap increase the exposure. Compare a synthetic sealant, which the guide puts at about three to six months, with a coating, which has a maker's stated life, a longer cure and a levelling window. Recommend the type that fits the owner's time and budget. Say that durability depends on parking and washing, and that the figure is the maker's. Do not promise lifetime protection, which the ACCC guidance says must be supported.

workedExamples.situation: A car is needed for a weekend show, and the owner wants a deep, wet gloss rather than long-term protection.
workedExamples.reasoning: A natural carnauba wax gives the deep, wet look the guide describes and suits a short-term show finish, with reapplication after the event. Apply it thinly, in shade, and allow the label's cure before handling the car. Record that it is a short-term finish, and that it will not last as long as a sealant or coating.

equipmentAndPpe: Applicator pads and microfibre towels, kept separate for wax, sealant and coating.
PPE: gloves suited to the product's SDS, with a latex-sensitivity check before use; eye protection; ventilation for solvent-based products, as the SDS requires.

commonErrors.error: Applying protection over swirls and contamination.
commonErrors.prevention: Decontaminate and polish first, and record the condition.
Spread thinly. More product does not add protection.

commonErrors.error: Removing the product too early or too late.
commonErrors.prevention: Follow the label's time. A late removal is much harder.

commonErrors.error: Degreasing a surface that protection is meant to bond to.
commonErrors.prevention: Use a degreaser only as the label and plan allow.
Keep to the cure time on the label.
State the maker's figure and the conditions it applies under.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Claims about protection must be accurate and supportable, and must not leave out material facts (ACCC: false or misleading claims).

Solvent-based coatings and some sealants have flash points and give off vapour. Read the SDS for flammability and ventilation. Dilution and cure times come from the label. Heat lamps used to speed cure are a heat hazard and need a separate risk assessment; this lesson does not adopt them.

qualityStandard: Protection type is chosen against the owner's use, and the reason is recorded.
Surface is clean and free of residue before application, and a touch check is recorded.
Cure and levelling times are followed, and no durability claim goes beyond the maker's figure.
documentationEvidence: Protection record: product, type, application method, cure time and owner instruction.
Written statement of the durability conditions given to the owner.
summary: Protection hides and shields; it does not repair.
Match the type to the owner's use, the time available and the paint's condition.
Apply thinly, observe the cure time, and state only the maker's durability.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which product is most likely to give a deep, wet look for a short show?
options: A natural carnauba wax, applied thinly
A coating applied and washed the next day

knowledgeChecks.question: A coating must be levelled within the window on the label. Why?
options: So the owner can watch the process from start to finish, and the reading is shown
Because coatings never need curing, so the level timing does not matter for the finish at all
A coating that dries too far before levelling can leave haze that may need polishing out
To remove the smell of the product from the paint and the cabin for the owner

knowledgeChecks.question: Which durability statement is supportable?
options: 'Durability depends on use and conditions; the figure is the maker's stated life.'
'It lasts forever, and no maintenance is needed for the life of the car.'
'It never needs polishing again, even after years of washing in direct sun and heavy use.'
'It lasts longer than any product on the market, so the owner can rely on it.'
